common_name: Karl Sax Forsythia (Tetraploid Large-Flowered Late-Blooming Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Karl Sax opens its bloom about two weeks later than most border forsythia, which can help buds dodge a hard late frost.

directions: Karl Sax was bred at the Arnold Arboretum as a tetraploid selection, giving it unusually large, deep golden-yellow flowers and a denser, bushier habit than most upright border forsythias. Its bloom opens roughly two weeks later than typical cultivars like Lynwood Gold, which can help the flowers escape a late hard freeze in variable-spring climates. Prune immediately after flowering, cutting a portion of the oldest canes to the ground every few years to keep the arching form open and floriferous. It tolerates a wide range of soils but colors and blooms best with full sun and even moisture.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in early spring in average, well-drained soil in sun to light shade; give Kumson some direct sun to keep its leaf pattern crisp, since heavy shade dulls the variegation.

directions: Kumson is grown less for its typical early-spring yellow flowers than for its striking foliage, with leaves netted in creamy white along the veins in a pattern unusual among forsythias, deepening toward pink and maroon tones as fall approaches. This gives the shrub a long season of ornamental interest well beyond the brief bloom period shared by other forsythia cultivars. Site it where its patterned leaves can be viewed up close, such as a border edge or foundation planting, and provide some direct sun since the reticulated pattern fades in heavier shade. Prune right after flowering only as needed to control size, since it forms an upright, arching, mounded shrub without regular shaping.

common_name: Arnold Dwarf Forsythia (Low Spreading Groundcover Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; give Arnold Dwarf plenty of lateral room since it spreads much wider than it grows tall, and be patient, as flowering is often sparse until the plant is several years established.

directions: Arnold Dwarf, a hybrid raised at the Arnold Arboretum, is grown chiefly as a low, wide-spreading ground-covering shrub rather than for a heavy floral display, since its pale yellow flowers are typically sparse and may not appear at all for the first several seasons after planting. Where its arching branches touch the soil they will root in, gradually knitting together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat useful on slopes and banks for erosion control. Foliage takes on a bronze cast in autumn, adding some seasonal interest beyond the modest spring bloom. It needs only occasional thinning of old wood to stay tidy and tolerates a wide range of well-drained soils.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Week-End's compact size makes it a good fit for foundation plantings and informal hedges where standard border forsythias would quickly outgrow the space.

directions: Week-End is a Dutch-bred, compact border forsythia that packs the same bell-shaped, golden-yellow flowers of full-sized cultivars onto a dense, upright-arching shrub that tops out around four feet, roughly half the mature size of older varieties like Lynwood Gold. Bare stems flush completely with bloom in March before the leaves emerge, giving it the same explosive early-spring show as its larger relatives in a fraction of the space. Its dense, uniform habit suits it well to a low informal hedge, screen, or container planting on a patio. Prune right after flowering if size control is needed, since next year's buds set on the current season's new growth.

common_name: New Hampshire Gold Forsythia (Extreme Bud-Hardy Mounding Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; New Hampshire Gold is bred for exceptional flower-bud cold hardiness and is a reliable choice where standard forsythia cultivars often lose their buds to winter cold.

directions: New Hampshire Gold was bred by crossing Lynwood forsythia with the extremely hardy Forsythia ovata 'Ottawa', producing a mounded shrub whose flower buds tolerate winter lows well below zero without sacrificing bloom, unlike many border forsythia cultivars that flower unreliably after harsh winters. Single, deep golden-yellow flowers hang along the bare branches in earliest spring, and foliage can turn a notable deep red in fall in cold climates. Its rounded, mounding habit suits it to foundation plantings, mixed borders, and mass plantings in regions too cold for typical forsythia bloom. Full sun brings out the heaviest flowering, and it adapts to a wide range of well-drained soils with minimal care.
